questions.q: Which motives for cyberattacks appear in Lecture 1?
questions.title: Why attackers attack
questions.answer: The lecture groups common motives into financial gain, stealing information, curiosity or fun, and politically motivated disruption called hacktivism. A motive explains the attacker’s goal; it does not identify the exact technique used.
questions.teach: The same phishing technique could support different motives. A criminal may want money, while a state-sponsored group may want confidential research.
questions.example: A motive describes the result an attacker wants. Defenders use it with other evidence to understand likely targets and behavior.
questions.correct: Money, information theft, curiosity/fun, and hacktivism
distractors: Only hardware failure and weather
Faster software and lower costs
Backups, patching, and encryption

questions.q: Why is Stuxnet important in a defensive cybersecurity course?
questions.title: Stuxnet as a defense lesson
questions.answer: Stuxnet showed that malicious software can cross into an industrial environment, search for a specific target, manipulate physical equipment, and hide the change by presenting normal-looking readings. Defenders must protect operational technology and removable-media paths, not only internet-facing computers.
questions.teach: Stuxnet spread broadly but activated its damaging behavior only when it found the intended Siemens industrial setup. That distinction separates spreading from the final objective.
questions.example: A USB drive entering an isolated facility can create a path around an internet perimeter. Monitoring hosts and engineering systems still matters.
questions.correct: It linked a computer compromise to manipulated physical equipment
distractors: It was only a website advertisement
It proved isolated systems need no host defenses
It was a password manager for industrial users

questions.q: What does virtualization let a cybersecurity student do?
questions.title: Virtual machines and safe labs
questions.answer: Virtualization lets one physical computer run multiple simulated computers called virtual machines. A student can build isolated test systems, take snapshots, run controlled experiments, and return a VM to an earlier clean state. Isolation reduces risk but does not make unsafe activity harmless.
questions.teach: A snapshot records a VM state before a lab. After analyzing a sample in an authorized lab, the student can revert instead of rebuilding everything.
questions.example: The physical computer is the host. Each simulated computer is a guest VM. Network settings decide whether guests can reach the host, each other, or the internet.
questions.correct: Run isolated guest systems and restore earlier snapshots
distractors: Convert every attack into harmless text
Guarantee malware can never leave a guest
Replace the need for backups on production systems

questions.q: What is the central goal of defensive cybersecurity?
questions.title: Defense as a process
questions.answer: Defensive cybersecurity reduces the likelihood and impact of attacks by understanding threats, protecting systems, monitoring activity, investigating evidence, and recovering safely. One product cannot perform every part of that job.
questions.teach: A firewall may block an unwanted connection, but a defender still needs host safeguards, logs, user education, and a response plan.
questions.example: Picture a store: locks reduce entry risk, cameras provide evidence, staff report suspicious behavior, and a recovery plan explains what happens after an incident.
questions.correct: Use several coordinated safeguards to prevent, detect, investigate, and recover
distractors: Purchase one security product and stop monitoring
Focus only on attacks that already succeeded
Remove all users from every computer

questions.q: Why does secure architecture use more than one safeguard?
questions.title: Defense in depth and risk
questions.answer: Different safeguards cover different failure modes. Perimeter devices can filter traffic, host controls can restrict local actions, monitoring can reveal suspicious behavior, and recovery controls can limit damage. The chosen protection should reflect asset value, risk, and available resources.
questions.teach: If a malicious attachment reaches a laptop, limited privileges and application controls may still stop it after an email filter missed it.
questions.example: A castle with several walls illustrates the idea: crossing one boundary does not immediately expose everything behind it.
questions.correct: One missed attack can still meet another independent safeguard
distractors: Every safeguard detects exactly the same event
Multiple safeguards eliminate all residual risk
Security budgets do not affect architecture

questions.q: What are choke points and monitoring visibility?
questions.title: Choke points and visibility
questions.answer: A choke point is a network location through which important traffic must pass, making consistent inspection possible. Visibility means defenders can observe useful activity at internet gateways and inside the network. Poor placement can leave blind spots.
questions.teach: Monitoring only the internet edge may miss traffic between two compromised internal computers. Internal sensors add another view.
questions.example: A building with one staffed entrance creates a choke point. Cameras inside provide visibility after someone enters.
questions.correct: They create inspectable paths and useful views of network activity
distractors: They encrypt every stored file automatically
They remove the need for internal monitoring
They make every system use one password

questions.q: Which design qualities must a secure network balance?
questions.title: Availability, scalability, and security
questions.answer: A network should remain available when needed, scale as demand grows, protect its systems and data, interoperate with required technology, stay manageable, and fit financial constraints. Maximizing one quality without considering the others can create an unusable design.
questions.teach: A security appliance that cannot handle peak traffic may become a bottleneck and reduce availability even when its filtering works.
questions.example: A company plans growth from 100 to 1,000 users. Capacity and administrative effort must grow without discarding essential protections.
questions.correct: Security must work together with availability, growth, management, and cost
distractors: Security is the only design quality that matters
Availability means every user gets administrator rights
Scalability means removing traffic inspection

questions.q: How do firewalls and router access-control lists protect a network?
questions.title: Firewalls and router ACLs
questions.answer: Both can allow or block traffic according to rules such as source, destination, protocol, and port. Routers primarily connect networks and may apply ACLs. Firewalls specialize in enforcing security policy and may track connection state or inspect more context.
questions.teach: A rule may allow HTTPS from the internet to one public web server while blocking direct access to an internal database.
questions.example: The rule is like a guest list that names which traffic may enter which door. Broad rules admit more than narrow rules.
questions.correct: They enforce traffic rules at network boundaries
distractors: They guarantee that allowed applications contain no malware
They replace authentication inside every application
They store a complete copy of every packet forever

questions.q: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
questions.title: IDS versus IPS
questions.answer: An Intrusion Detection System observes activity and alerts when it recognizes a signature or anomaly. An Intrusion Prevention System can sit in the traffic path and block or modify traffic as well as alert. Prevention can stop harm but a mistaken block can interrupt legitimate work.
questions.teach: An IDS reports a suspicious exploit attempt for an analyst. An inline IPS can drop that traffic before it reaches the target.
questions.example: A burglar alarm resembles detection. A locked gate that refuses entry resembles prevention. Both require accurate rules and review.
questions.correct: An IDS alerts; an IPS can also block traffic
distractors: An IDS encrypts while an IPS performs backups
An IDS runs only on laptops and an IPS only in clouds
An IDS allows all traffic and never records events

questions.q: What security job does a web proxy perform?
questions.title: Proxy servers
questions.answer: A proxy acts as an intermediary between a user and a destination service. A web proxy can apply organizational policy, inspect requests, and block categories or known malicious sites before the user connects directly.
questions.teach: When a user requests a known malware domain, the proxy can return a block page instead of retrieving the site.
questions.example: The browser talks to the proxy; the proxy evaluates the request and, if allowed, communicates with the website on the user’s behalf.
questions.correct: It evaluates and mediates user web requests
distractors: It assigns every computer a permanent MAC address
It proves every unblocked website is safe forever
It replaces disk encryption

questions.q: How do antivirus, host IPS, and application allowlisting differ?
questions.title: Host protection and application allowlisting
questions.answer: Antivirus looks for known or suspicious malicious software. Host IPS watches local events and can act on host-specific rules. Application allowlisting permits approved software and blocks unapproved programs by default. Each can miss activity that another catches.
questions.teach: A new unapproved executable may have no antivirus signature. Allowlisting can still prevent it from launching because it is absent from the approved list.
questions.example: Antivirus asks whether a file appears bad. Allowlisting asks whether the organization approved it to run. Host IPS watches what occurs on the device.
questions.correct: They use different evidence and policies to protect the endpoint
distractors: All three are names for the same firewall rule
All three only inspect traffic at the internet router
All three guarantee no false positives

questions.q: What is the difference between packet capture and flow data?
questions.title: Full packet capture versus flow data
questions.answer: Full packet capture can preserve packet contents and headers for detailed investigation, but it needs substantial storage and may contain sensitive data. Flow data summarizes who communicated with whom, when, for how long, and often how much data moved, without preserving the complete conversation.
questions.teach: Flow may show a laptop contacted a server for ten minutes. Packet capture may show the protocol details and unencrypted content exchanged during that connection.
questions.example: A phone bill resembles flow records. A recording of the call resembles full content capture.
questions.correct: Flow summarizes connections; packet capture can preserve packet-level detail
distractors: Flow contains every file while capture contains only IP addresses
Packet capture cannot support investigations
Flow automatically blocks every listed connection

questions.q: How do DDoS attacks interfere with availability?
questions.title: DDoS, SYN floods, and Slowloris
questions.answer: A Distributed Denial of Service attack uses many sources or requests to exhaust a service or its network so legitimate users cannot receive service. A SYN flood consumes connection-handling resources. Slowloris keeps many incomplete requests open slowly. Defenses depend on the traffic pattern and may involve providers, filtering, capacity, and timeouts.
questions.teach: A SYN flood sends many connection starts without completing the handshake. Slowloris sends enough partial data to keep sessions waiting.
questions.example: Both attacks occupy limited service capacity, but one can flood quickly while the other holds resources open.
questions.correct: They consume limited network or server capacity needed by real users
distractors: They secretly change database queries without affecting availability
They only work after a user reveals a password
They encrypt backups for confidentiality

questions.q: What makes SQL injection possible, and how should developers prevent it?
questions.title: SQL injection
questions.answer: SQL injection occurs when an application treats untrusted input as part of a database command. The primary defense is to keep data separate from command structure by using parameterized queries, supported by input validation, least privilege, testing, and monitoring. A web application firewall can add protection but does not repair unsafe code.
questions.teach: A login value should become a data parameter. Concatenating it into a SQL command may let crafted text change the command’s meaning.
questions.example: The database must receive the query structure separately from the user-supplied value so the value cannot become an instruction.
questions.correct: The application mixes untrusted input into a database command
distractors: The database has too many encrypted backups
A router uses a long ACL
A user opens two browser tabs

questions.q: What happens in a cross-site scripting attack?
questions.title: Cross-site scripting
questions.answer: Cross-site scripting occurs when a web application places untrusted content into a page without the context-appropriate output encoding or other safeguards. A victim’s browser may then execute attacker-controlled script in the trusted site’s context. Defenses include output encoding, safe APIs, content security policy, validation, and secure cookie settings.
questions.teach: A comment field stores attacker-controlled script. When another user views the comment, the browser may run it as part of the site.
questions.example: SQL injection targets a database command. XSS targets content that the browser interprets. Both start with unsafe handling of untrusted data.
questions.correct: A trusted page causes a browser to execute attacker-controlled script
distractors: A router runs out of cable ports
A disk uses full encryption
A DNS server assigns a local address

questions.q: What is website defacement?
questions.title: Website defacement
questions.answer: Website defacement is an unauthorized change to visible website content, often used for embarrassment, messaging, or notoriety. Attackers may exploit vulnerable software or stolen credentials. Defenders patch systems, protect accounts, restrict write permissions, monitor changes, and maintain recoverable content.
questions.teach: An attacker gains access to a content-management account and replaces the homepage. The visual change is the symptom; the account compromise is the access path.
questions.example: Restoring the page without fixing the exploited weakness allows the attacker to change it again.
questions.correct: An attacker changes site content without authorization
distractors: A user changes browser zoom
A server compresses an image
A company publishes an approved redesign

questions.q: How does an advance-fee scam manipulate a victim?
questions.title: Advance-fee and 419 scams
questions.answer: The scam promises money, a prize, or another benefit, then gradually requests personal information or payment to release it. Attackers may begin with harmless-looking questions to build trust before seeking bank details or fees. Victims should stop contact, preserve evidence, and report through appropriate channels.
questions.teach: A false lottery notice asks for contact information first, then later demands a processing payment. The staged requests lower suspicion.
questions.example: The key pattern is an unexpected reward combined with a request to pay or disclose information before receiving it.
questions.correct: It promises a benefit and then requests money or sensitive information
distractors: It patches a workstation automatically
It blocks a website category at a proxy
It encrypts a legitimate bank transfer

questions.q: Why must defenders separate an attack from the weakness it uses?
questions.title: Attack, vulnerability, and defense
questions.answer: An attack is the harmful action or attempt. A vulnerability is a weakness that may enable it. A defense reduces likelihood or impact. Naming these separately helps teams choose a control that addresses the actual path instead of the visible symptom alone.
questions.teach: SQL injection is an attack technique. Unsafe query construction is the vulnerability. Parameterized queries address that weakness.
questions.example: If water enters through a broken window, removing the water handles the result; repairing the window addresses the path.
questions.correct: The weakness determines which safeguard can interrupt the attack path
distractors: Every attack uses the same software weakness
A visible symptom always reveals the root cause
Defenses only matter after data is stolen

questions.q: What makes a message a phishing attempt?
questions.title: Phishing, smishing, and vishing
questions.answer: Phishing uses a deceptive message to persuade a person to disclose information, open a harmful file, install software, send money, or visit a false site. The channel can be email or instant messaging; smishing uses text messages and vishing uses voice calls.
questions.teach: A message impersonates payroll and links to a false login page. The attacker wants the victim to supply credentials.
questions.example: The attack targets human trust. A professional logo or familiar name does not prove the sender or destination is legitimate.
questions.correct: It uses deception to make a person take an unsafe action
distractors: It passively records every packet on a switch
It automatically patches a browser
It verifies a digital signature

questions.q: How is spear phishing different from broad phishing?
questions.title: Spear phishing
questions.answer: Spear phishing targets selected people with details chosen to appear relevant or trustworthy. The attacker may research a person’s role, coworkers, current events, or projects. Broad phishing sends a similar lure to many recipients and waits for someone to respond.
questions.teach: A forged message to one finance employee refers to a real executive and current vendor. The specificity makes the request more believable.
questions.example: “Spear” describes the narrow target. A convincing message still needs independent verification through a trusted channel.
questions.correct: It is tailored to a specific person or small group
distractors: It can only be delivered by postal mail
It never includes a link or attachment
It is an untargeted message sent identically to everyone

questions.q: What can an email header help an investigator determine?
questions.title: Email headers and investigation
questions.answer: Header fields can show routing hops, timestamps, message identifiers, authentication results, and addresses used during delivery. Analysts compare them with the visible sender and organizational records. Headers provide evidence, but individual fields can be forged or misunderstood.
questions.teach: A display name says “Payroll,” while authentication results and the sending domain point elsewhere. That mismatch supports further investigation.
questions.example: Read Received lines with time zones and direction in mind. Preserve the original message because forwarding can alter or hide useful header data.
questions.correct: The technical path and authentication evidence associated with delivery
distractors: The sender’s intent with absolute certainty
Every file the sender has ever opened
The recipient’s operating-system password

questions.q: What is the safest way to verify an unexpected account message?
questions.title: Responding safely to suspicious messages
questions.answer: Avoid the supplied link or phone number. Open the organization’s known app or type its trusted address yourself, or contact the organization using a separately verified number. Report the suspicious message and preserve it according to policy.
questions.teach: A banking message says an account is locked. Open the bank’s known app instead of using the message link.
questions.example: Verification needs an independent path. Contact information inside the suspicious message remains under the sender’s control.
questions.correct: Use a trusted channel obtained independently of the message
distractors: Reply and ask whether the sender is malicious
Open the link if the logo looks correct
Disable antivirus before opening the attachment

questions.q: How does fake antivirus software pressure a victim?
questions.title: Fake antivirus and scareware
questions.answer: Scareware presents alarming claims about infections or disk problems, then pressures the user to install software or pay for a false fix. The installed program may steal information, weaken real protection, or create more pop-ups. Use approved security tools and support channels.
questions.teach: A browser pop-up announces hundreds of infections and demands immediate payment. A webpage cannot be trusted simply because it resembles a system scanner.
questions.example: Urgency and fear push the user past normal verification. Close the prompt safely and ask support to inspect the device if installation occurred.
questions.correct: It invents or exaggerates danger to trigger installation or payment
distractors: It quietly improves disk performance for free
It is an operating-system patch from every vendor
It verifies that a website certificate is valid

questions.q: Why is a fake disk defragmenter a security problem?
questions.title: Fake disk tools
questions.answer: A fake disk utility displays invented errors and asks the victim to buy or install a supposed repair. It uses the same social-pressure pattern as rogue antivirus and may install malware or collect payment information.
questions.teach: The program reports critical disk errors immediately after a user visits a suspicious site, even though it never performed a trustworthy scan.
questions.example: A realistic interface is only appearance. Verify alerts through the operating system or an approved support process.
questions.correct: It uses false system errors to sell or install an unsafe product
distractors: It reorganizes approved files under administrator supervision
It creates a verified offline backup
It checks a signed operating-system update

questions.q: Why do technical controls and user awareness work together?
questions.title: User awareness and reconnaissance
questions.answer: Filters and endpoint controls can block many lures, but attackers change content and research targets. Users need a clear way to recognize unusual requests, verify them, and report them. Defenders also need to understand reconnaissance because public details can make a targeted message more convincing.
questions.teach: A filter allows a new sender. An employee notices the unusual payment request and calls the known manager instead of acting.
questions.example: Technology reduces exposure while trained human judgment can interrupt a message that passes automated checks.
questions.correct: Each can catch suspicious activity the other misses
distractors: Training makes mail filters unnecessary
A mail filter can determine every human intention
Reconnaissance only examines physical buildings

questions.q: What does operating-system hardening mean?
questions.title: Operating-system hardening
questions.answer: Operating-system hardening means changing a host’s configuration to reduce its attack surface and limit damage. Common steps include timely patching, limited user privileges, removing unneeded services, enabling host firewalls, using endpoint protection, and applying tested security settings.
questions.teach: A workstation does not need a remote service, so an administrator disables it and closes the related listening port.
questions.example: Hardening removes unnecessary opportunities and strengthens the functions that must remain. It is an ongoing process as software and needs change.
questions.correct: Reducing unnecessary exposure and strengthening required functions
distractors: Adding every optional service for future use
Giving all users administrator access
Disabling updates so settings never change

questions.q: Why do organizations test patches before broad deployment?
questions.title: Patching safely
questions.answer: Patches correct known defects and vulnerabilities, but a change may conflict with an application or configuration. Organizations obtain trusted updates, test them on representative systems, plan deployment and rollback, install them according to risk, and verify the result.
questions.teach: A security patch works on a test workstation but breaks a required legacy application. Testing reveals the compatibility problem before every employee is affected.
questions.example: Delay also carries risk because known vulnerabilities remain exposed. Teams balance urgency with controlled testing and compensating safeguards.
questions.correct: Testing can reveal compatibility or operational problems before production rollout
distractors: Testing proves attackers cannot use any future vulnerability
A tested patch never needs verification after installation
Testing replaces the need to obtain the patch from a trusted source

questions.q: How does using a non-administrator account reduce damage?
questions.title: Least privilege and reverse shells
questions.answer: Least privilege gives a user or process only the permissions needed for approved work. If malicious code runs under that account, it may have less ability to change protected files or security settings. A reverse shell makes the compromised host initiate a command channel outward, sometimes through commonly allowed traffic.
questions.teach: A user can edit documents but cannot install a system driver. Malware launched by that user encounters the same permission boundary unless it exploits another weakness.
questions.example: Least privilege limits authority; it does not prevent every compromise. Egress monitoring and host controls help detect or restrict unauthorized outbound command channels.
questions.correct: Malicious code initially receives fewer powerful permissions
distractors: The account cannot connect to any network
The user automatically becomes an administrator during attacks
Every reverse shell uses an inbound blocked port only

questions.q: How do disabled services and host firewalls reduce attack surface?
questions.title: Services, updates, and host firewalls
questions.answer: An unnecessary service creates code, a listening path, and configuration that the host does not need. Disabling it removes that opportunity. A host firewall restricts which remaining services may receive or send traffic. Automatic updates can reduce exposure time when the organization has an appropriate testing and deployment process.
questions.teach: A database server should not expose a file-sharing service nobody uses. Disable it rather than relying only on a perimeter firewall.
questions.example: The host firewall follows the device across networks and can restrict local traffic that never crosses the internet firewall.
questions.correct: They remove unused entry points and restrict access to required ones
distractors: They make passwords and account controls unnecessary
They guarantee every allowed service is free of bugs
They turn a workstation into a network router

questions.q: How do antivirus and host IPS contribute to hardening?
questions.title: Antivirus versus host IPS
questions.answer: Antivirus detects known or suspicious malicious software. Host IPS watches events on one machine and can apply detailed behavioral or pattern rules. Both add layers, but they require updates, tuning, and review. False positives are legitimate events incorrectly flagged as threats.
questions.teach: A host IPS rule alerts when an unusual program creates a file in a protected system folder. Antivirus may separately identify the file’s known malicious signature.
questions.example: Detailed host rules increase visibility but also generate noise. Analysts must distinguish useful signals from routine activity.
questions.correct: They inspect different host evidence and can detect different suspicious behavior
distractors: They physically disconnect every infected cable
They replace all operating-system permissions
They only protect public websites

questions.q: How can organizations enforce and validate workstation hardening?
questions.title: Browser controls, hardening guides, and NAC
questions.answer: Organizations can use secure baselines and hardening guides, configuration policy, browser restrictions, endpoint tools, and Network Access Control. Changes should be applied in manageable groups and tested so administrators can trace compatibility failures. NAC can check device posture before granting normal network access.
questions.teach: A laptop missing required patches connects to the network. NAC places it in a restricted remediation area until it meets policy.
questions.example: A long checklist does not prove the system works securely. Apply settings deliberately, test required work, and monitor whether devices stay compliant.
questions.correct: Use tested baselines and posture checks to keep devices within policy
distractors: Apply hundreds of settings at once without testing
Let users disable every safeguard permanently
Use NAC only to increase monitor brightness

questions.q: Why can the same website be safe one day and malicious another?
questions.title: Website safety changes over time
questions.answer: A legitimate site can be compromised, an advertisement or external script can change, or a malicious site can be cleaned. Reputation and scan results describe a point in time. Defenders combine current evidence and avoid treating an earlier clean result as a permanent guarantee.
questions.teach: A news site is safe in the morning, then an attacker changes one included script in the afternoon. Yesterday’s scan cannot evaluate the new content.
questions.example: A website is a changing collection of first-party and third-party resources. The domain name alone does not describe every resource loaded now.
questions.correct: Website content and third-party resources can change after an earlier scan
distractors: A domain name changes every second by definition
HTTPS guarantees all page content is harmless
A clean result deletes all future vulnerabilities

questions.q: What does an analyst inspect during a manual website review?
questions.title: Manual source review
questions.answer: The analyst examines HTML, scripts, redirects, embedded frames, downloads, and obfuscated code for behavior that does not fit the site. An iframe is not automatically malicious, and JavaScript is not automatically malicious; context and destination matter.
questions.teach: A hidden iframe loads a newly registered external domain and starts a download. Those combined facts justify deeper isolated analysis.
questions.example: Manual review can reveal logic that an automated tool misses, but opening active content on a normal workstation can expose the analyst.
questions.correct: Page code, embedded resources, redirects, and suspicious behavior
distractors: Only the color and font of the homepage
Only whether the domain uses HTTPS
The visitor’s private password database

questions.q: What are the strengths and limits of automated website-analysis tools?
questions.title: Automated website analysis
questions.answer: Automated scanners and reputation services can quickly compare a site with known patterns, behavior, and reports. They scale better than manual review but can miss new attacks, produce false results, or evaluate a different moment and environment. Analysts should treat results as evidence, not proof.
questions.teach: Two scanners report no known malware, but the site only delivers harmful code to one browser version. The scan reduces uncertainty without eliminating it.
questions.example: A reputation score depends on prior observation. A new malicious domain may not have a history yet.
questions.correct: They provide fast evidence but can miss new or conditional behavior
distractors: They guarantee a site stays safe forever
They make isolation unnecessary for suspicious content
They can determine a human attacker’s identity from the page color

questions.q: Why use a virtual machine to investigate a suspicious site?
questions.title: Isolated dynamic testing
questions.answer: An isolated VM can mimic a target environment while monitoring file, registry, process, and network changes. A snapshot supports recovery after an authorized test. Analysts still restrict network access, avoid real credentials, protect the host, and follow policy because isolation can fail.
questions.teach: The analyst opens a suspect page in a disposable guest, records its outbound connections, and reverts to the clean snapshot after collecting evidence.
questions.example: Dynamic analysis observes what content actually does. Static source review reads code without executing it. Each can reveal evidence the other misses.
questions.correct: It contains the experiment and lets the analyst observe system changes
distractors: It guarantees legal authorization for any website
It makes malware unable to contact any network automatically
It proves a clean host needs no backup

questions.q: What should a defender do before interacting with a suspicious website?
questions.title: Safe investigation decisions
questions.answer: First confirm authorization and whether interaction is necessary. Use existing reputation and passive evidence when sufficient. If active testing is required, use an approved isolated environment, restrict connectivity, capture evidence, and never enter real credentials.
questions.teach: A user reports a suspicious link. The analyst checks the message and approved intelligence sources before deciding whether a controlled visit adds value.
questions.example: Curiosity does not justify exposure. Investigation should answer a defined question with the least risky method that can answer it.
questions.correct: Define the question and use the least risky authorized method
distractors: Open it on a production administrator workstation
Forward it to coworkers to compare results
Enter a real password to see whether login works

questions.q: How are plaintext, ciphertext, encryption, decryption, a cipher, and a key connected?
questions.title: Encryption vocabulary
questions.answer: Plaintext is the readable input. A cipher is the algorithm that combines plaintext with a key to produce ciphertext. Decryption uses the appropriate key and algorithm to recover plaintext. Security should rely on protecting keys and using reviewed algorithms, not hiding the algorithm.
questions.teach: A file begins as readable plaintext. Encryption transforms it into ciphertext. An authorized recipient uses the required key to decrypt it.
questions.example: The algorithm is like a known lock design; the key controls who can perform the authorized transformation.
questions.correct: A cipher and key transform plaintext into ciphertext
distractors: A hash key converts ciphertext directly into a password
Plaintext is already unreadable encrypted output
Decryption permanently destroys all original data

questions.q: Which security properties can cryptography support?
questions.title: What cryptography can protect
questions.answer: Cryptography can support confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation, and obfuscation in appropriate designs. It can protect data at rest and in transit; protecting data while actively in use is harder because an authorized process needs access to it.
questions.teach: Encryption protects a stored file’s confidentiality. A verified digital signature can support integrity, sender authentication, and non-repudiation.
questions.example: One mechanism does not automatically supply every property. Encryption alone does not prove who created a message.
questions.correct: Confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and related assurances
distractors: Unlimited availability with no redundancy
Physical cooling for every server
Automatic deletion of every backup

questions.q: What does a cryptographic hash do?
questions.title: Hashing and collisions
questions.answer: A hash function maps input of any length to a fixed-length digest. Defenders compare digests to detect changes. Hashing is designed as a one-way operation and does not provide decryption. A collision occurs when different inputs produce the same digest; obsolete algorithms with practical collision weaknesses should not be used for collision-sensitive security.
questions.teach: A vendor publishes a trusted file hash. After download, you compute the file’s hash and compare it with the trusted value to detect alteration.
questions.example: A digest is a fingerprint for comparison, not an encrypted copy of the file. You cannot reconstruct the full file from the digest.
questions.correct: It creates a fixed-length digest used to compare data
distractors: It creates ciphertext that every user can decrypt without a key
It guarantees two inputs can never share a digest
It compresses a file and stores every original byte

questions.q: How do stream and block ciphers process data differently?
questions.title: Stream and block ciphers
questions.answer: A stream cipher processes a stream in small units, while a block cipher transforms fixed-size blocks. Secure use depends on the full construction, including modes, nonces, key handling, and authentication, rather than the category name alone.
questions.teach: A block cipher may need a defined mode to protect a message longer than one block. Reusing a nonce in a mode that requires uniqueness can break security.
questions.example: The processing unit differs, but both still require an approved design and correct implementation.

questions.q: How does symmetric encryption work?
questions.title: Symmetric encryption
questions.answer: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key, or directly related shared secret, for encryption and decryption. It is efficient for large amounts of data, but authorized parties need a secure method to share and protect the secret key.
questions.teach: A disk-encryption system uses a symmetric data-encryption key because large files must be processed efficiently.
questions.example: Anyone who obtains the shared key may decrypt protected data and possibly create convincing ciphertext, so key distribution and storage matter.
questions.correct: The authorized parties use the same shared secret key
distractors: Everyone encrypts with a public key and only a private key decrypts
No key is required after installation
The digest is reversed to recover plaintext

questions.q: How do public and private keys work together?
questions.title: Asymmetric encryption and signatures
questions.answer: Asymmetric cryptography uses a mathematically related key pair. A public key may be shared while the private key remains controlled by its owner. Depending on the scheme, the pair supports encryption or digital signatures. For a signature, the private key creates the signature and the public key verifies it.
questions.teach: A software vendor signs an update with its private key. A device uses the vendor’s trusted public key to verify the signature before installation.
questions.example: A valid signature supports source and integrity claims. It does not hide the signed data unless encryption is also used.
questions.correct: The private key signs and the corresponding public key verifies
distractors: The public key must stay secret while the private key is posted
Both keys are identical copies
A signature automatically encrypts every signed message

questions.q: What is a downgrade attack?
questions.title: Cryptographic attacks and downgrade risk
questions.answer: A downgrade attack forces systems to fall back from a stronger protocol or algorithm to an older weaker option. Defenders disable deprecated choices, require safe minimum versions, and monitor failed negotiation. Collision attacks are different: they seek distinct inputs with the same hash.
questions.teach: A client and server both support a modern protocol, but an attacker interferes so they negotiate an obsolete version with known weaknesses.
questions.example: Compatibility fallbacks can create an attack path. Supporting a strong option does not help if an attacker can force the weak one.
questions.correct: It forces communication to use an older weaker security option
distractors: It adds a longer key to every connection
It restores a VM snapshot
It finds a website through DNS

questions.q: Where can encryption be applied?
questions.title: Software and hardware encryption
questions.answer: Encryption can protect individual files, file systems, full disks, removable drives, databases, and communications. Hardware modules such as TPMs and HSMs can protect keys or perform cryptographic operations. The appropriate control depends on the threat and what happens while the system is running.
questions.teach: Full-disk encryption protects a stolen powered-off laptop, but an already unlocked laptop may expose files to the signed-in user or running malware.
questions.example: Encryption at rest does not replace account security, backups, or protection while data is actively used.
questions.correct: At file, disk, device, database, and communication layers
distractors: Only inside public web pages
Only after data has been deleted
Only on computers without operating systems

questions.q: How does a blockchain connect records?
questions.title: Blocks, hash pointers, and Merkle trees
questions.answer: A blockchain organizes transactions into blocks. A block header contains metadata and a hash reference to earlier data. Changing an earlier block changes its hash and breaks later references unless they are recomputed under the network’s rules. A Merkle tree combines transaction hashes into one root used to verify membership efficiently.
questions.teach: To prove a transaction belongs to a block, a node can provide the transaction and a path of neighboring hashes leading to the recorded Merkle root.
questions.example: Hash links make changes evident; consensus rules determine which proposed history participants accept. Hashing alone does not make false input truthful.
questions.correct: Each block references prior data with hashes and summarizes transactions with a Merkle root
distractors: Every block stores only an unencrypted password
One central spreadsheet decides all peer actions
A hash pointer hides every transaction from all participants

questions.q: Why does a distributed blockchain need consensus?
questions.title: Consensus, mining, forks, and P2P
questions.answer: Participants need rules for agreeing on an accepted transaction history when messages, faults, and competing blocks exist. Proof-of-work mining searches for a nonce that satisfies a target and is difficult to find but easy to verify. A protocol change without shared adoption can create a fork.
questions.teach: Two miners publish blocks at similar times. Nodes follow the protocol’s chain-selection rule until one history gains the required preference.
questions.example: Peer-to-peer distribution spreads data and work across nodes. It does not mean every node makes an independent history with no agreement rules.
questions.correct: It gives nodes rules for selecting a shared accepted history
distractors: It makes every transaction legal automatically
It prevents all software changes
It stores every private key in one central node

questions.q: What jobs do TCP and IP perform?
questions.title: Packets, TCP, and IP
questions.answer: IP provides addressing and routing for packets across networks. TCP runs above IP and provides a connection-oriented byte stream with ordering, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control. A packet also carries control information in headers; the application data is the payload.
questions.teach: A browser sends data through TCP. IP routers forward the resulting packets. The receiver’s TCP reorders data and detects missing portions for retransmission.
questions.example: IP helps data reach the destination host. TCP helps the endpoints exchange an ordered reliable stream. They cooperate but solve different problems.
questions.correct: IP routes packets; TCP provides reliable ordered transport
distractors: TCP assigns website names while IP encrypts disks
IP guarantees application authentication
TCP stores every packet permanently

questions.q: What evidence can a packet analyzer provide?
questions.title: Spoofing, scanning, and Wireshark
questions.answer: A packet analyzer such as Wireshark captures and decodes traffic visible to the selected interface. Analysts can inspect addresses, ports, flags, timing, protocol fields, and unencrypted payloads. It does not automatically prove who physically operated a source, because addresses can be spoofed or traffic can pass through compromised hosts.
questions.teach: Repeated SYN packets to many ports may indicate scanning. The pattern supports an interpretation when combined with context and logs.
questions.example: A capture sees what reached its collection point. Traffic elsewhere, encrypted content, or dropped traffic may be absent.
questions.correct: Protocol fields and timing for traffic visible at the capture point
distractors: Every event on networks the interface cannot observe
The real human identity behind every IP address
Plaintext from every encrypted session without keys

questions.q: Why are application protocols part of network defense?
questions.title: TCP/IP protocols and security
questions.answer: The TCP/IP suite includes many application protocols, each with its own purpose and security properties. Defenders must know what a protocol exposes, whether it authenticates peers or encrypts data, and which ports and systems should use it. A protocol’s presence alone does not prove malicious activity.
questions.teach: FTP can transfer files but sends sensitive information without encryption in its basic form. A secure alternative changes the protection of the connection.
questions.example: Traffic rules should follow actual business need. Blocking every unfamiliar protocol can break work; allowing every protocol expands exposure.
questions.correct: Protocols define how services communicate and what protections they provide
distractors: Every application protocol automatically encrypts data
Protocols only affect physical cables
One port number proves the user’s identity

questions.q: How are SNMP and ICMP used differently?
questions.title: SNMP and ICMP
questions.answer: Simple Network Management Protocol lets administrators query and manage network-device information through agents and management data. SNMPv3 adds authentication and privacy features absent from older community-string designs. ICMP supports network control and diagnostic messages; ping commonly uses ICMP to test reachability and measure response time.
questions.teach: A monitoring system uses SNMP to read interface counters and CPU use, while ping checks whether the device responds and how long replies take.
questions.example: A community string acts like a shared secret in older SNMP versions and should not be treated as strong modern protection.
questions.correct: SNMP reads management data; ICMP supports reachability and network diagnostics
distractors: SNMP transfers email while ICMP encrypts disks
ICMP manages device configuration databases
They are two names for HTTPS

questions.q: What problem does DNSSEC address?
questions.title: DNS and DNSSEC
questions.answer: DNS maps names to records such as IP addresses. DNS poisoning attempts to supply false answers so users reach an unintended destination. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures that let a validating resolver check that DNS data came from the signed zone and was not altered. DNSSEC does not encrypt DNS queries or prove a website itself is harmless.
questions.teach: An attacker supplies a false address for a bank name. A validating resolver rejects the answer when its signature chain does not verify.
questions.example: DNSSEC protects authenticity and integrity of DNS data. HTTPS separately protects the web connection when correctly validated.
questions.correct: It helps resolvers detect forged or altered DNS answers
distractors: It hides every DNS query from the network
It scans the destination for malware
It assigns administrator rights to domain owners

questions.q: Why is basic FTP unsafe for sensitive transfers?
questions.title: FTP, FTPS, and secure file transfer
questions.answer: Basic File Transfer Protocol does not encrypt credentials or file contents, allowing interception on the network. FTPS wraps FTP with TLS. SFTP is a different protocol carried through SSH. Active and passive FTP also differ in how the data connection is established, which affects firewall behavior.
questions.teach: A user sends a password over basic FTP on an untrusted network. Someone capturing the traffic may read it.
questions.example: Similar names do not mean identical protocols. FTPS extends FTP; SFTP uses SSH and has different ports and behavior.
questions.correct: Basic FTP transmits credentials and content without encryption
distractors: FTP automatically signs every transferred file
FTP uses full-disk encryption for the server
FTP prevents all man-in-the-middle attacks

questions.q: Which secure protocols match common network activities?
questions.title: Secure email and application protocols
questions.answer: HTTPS protects web traffic with TLS. S/MIME can sign or encrypt email content using certificates. SRTP protects real-time audio or video. SSH provides secure remote command access and tunneling. A secure protocol still depends on valid keys, certificates, configuration, and endpoint security.
questions.teach: An administrator uses SSH instead of Telnet so credentials and commands are not sent as readable plaintext.
questions.example: Encryption protects data on the connection. It cannot make a malicious server trustworthy or repair an infected endpoint by itself.
questions.correct: HTTPS for web, SSH for remote administration, and S/MIME for protected email content
distractors: FTP for password secrecy and HTTP for private web traffic
ICMP for email encryption and DNS for disk encryption
SNMPv1 for private file transfer

questions.q: Why does security-device placement matter?
questions.title: Placement of security devices
questions.answer: A device can inspect or block only traffic that passes through its observation or enforcement point. Sensors and collectors belong where they can see relevant traffic. Inline prevention devices need capacity and safe failure behavior. Aggregation and correlation bring several views together but do not recover traffic that was never collected.
questions.teach: A sensor placed outside encryption termination sees encrypted bytes. A sensor after termination may inspect the application traffic, subject to privacy and access policy.
questions.example: Draw the traffic path first. Then place each control where its input actually crosses and where failure will not create unacceptable impact.
questions.correct: A control needs to sit on or observe the relevant traffic path
distractors: Every network location sees identical traffic
Placement only changes the color of a diagram
A sensor can reconstruct packets that never reached it

questions.q: What do security logs contribute to an investigation?
questions.title: Security logs and centralized analysis
questions.answer: Logs record events such as authentication attempts, requests, system errors, firewall decisions, and file changes. Analysts correlate timestamps, identities, addresses, and outcomes across sources. Central collection helps search and retention but requires time synchronization, access controls, storage planning, and normalization.
questions.teach: A firewall shows an inbound connection, an application log shows a failed login, and an audit log identifies the account action. Together they create a stronger timeline.
questions.example: A log entry is evidence from one system’s viewpoint. It may be incomplete, misconfigured, or use a different clock, so corroboration matters.
questions.correct: They preserve event evidence that can be correlated into a timeline
distractors: They prevent every logged attack automatically
They prove a failed login caused data theft
They replace the need to synchronize clocks

questions.q: What security benefits and risks come with virtualization?
questions.title: Virtualization security
questions.answer: Virtualization supports snapshots, isolated testing, rapid recovery, centralized management, and flexible capacity. Risks include hypervisor flaws, VM escape, weak separation, unpatched guest systems, uncontrolled VM copies, and concentration of many services on one host. Type 1 hypervisors run on hardware; Type 2 hypervisors run on a host operating system.
questions.teach: Ten server VMs share one physical host. Efficient management improves, but a host failure or hypervisor compromise can affect several services.
questions.example: A VM is still a computer that needs patching, access control, monitoring, and backup. A snapshot is not automatically a complete independent backup.
questions.correct: Virtualization improves isolation and recovery but concentrates new risks in hosts and hypervisors
distractors: Virtual machines require no patches
A Type 2 hypervisor has no host operating system
Snapshots guarantee off-site disaster recovery

questions.q: What changes when an organization uses cloud computing?
questions.title: Cloud models and shared security
questions.answer: Cloud providers deliver shared computing services through models such as SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS, and deployments may be public, private, community, or hybrid. Responsibility shifts by service model, but the customer still protects its data, identities, permissions, and configurations under its control.
questions.teach: With SaaS, the provider runs the application platform, while the customer decides which employees may access confidential records and how data is classified.
questions.example: Cloud means using someone else’s managed computing resources under an agreement. Physical systems still exist, and misconfiguration remains possible.
questions.correct: Some infrastructure duties shift, while customer data, identity, and configuration duties remain
distractors: The provider becomes responsible for every customer password choice
Cloud data no longer resides on computers
Using SaaS removes the need for access reviews
